name: Ika Igbo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Uguru, Joy Oluchi. 2015. Ika Igbo (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 45(2): 213-219. doi:10.1017/S0025100315000067
catalog_locator: pp. 216-217, section 'Intonation system'; also p. 213 'Ika manifests intonation in addition to lexical tone.'
catalog_quote: Both tone (use of pitch variation in distinguishing words lexically or grammatically) and intonation (use of pitch variation mainly for expressing emotions and attitudes) feature in Ika. There are two major tones: high and low. The third, downstep, is not a major tone but a downstepped high. ... Like in any tone language, tone distinguishes between words in Ika, as can be seen in the minimal sets below. ... Intonation is one of the major features in which Ika phonology differs from many Igbo dialects. Intonation involves the use of to express various meanings, for example attitudinal and emotional, and to mark syntactic form. Also, in the use of intonation, an utterance has only one prominent syllable (the nuclear syllable). These two features are observed in Ika but not in the Standard or other Igbo dialects.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ika is a two-tone language (H, L, plus downstep) in which every syllable bears a lexical tone; there is no word-level stress rule. Prominence exists only at the level of the intonation group: each utterance (intonation group) has a single prominent nuclear syllable that carries one of six intonation tunes. Uguru 2014 (abstract only) calls this nucleus 'a stressed syllable' and states that any other degrees of stress are subsumed under tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the 2015 Illustration; Uguru 2014 abstract: 'Other degrees of stress are subsumed under tone since every syllable bears a tone.'
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Tonal changes, losses and masking occur at nuclear syllables (Uguru 2014 abstract).
new_statements.domain_note: Utterance / intonation-group domain, not word. The 2015 Illustration is based on one 50-year-old female speaker (the author) reading isolated words and a passage. Supporting statement from Uguru 2014 abstract (OpenAIRE record saved): 'Hence in Ika, every intonation group (or tonal intonation group) has a nucleus (a stressed syllable) and it is this nucleus that bears the intonation. [..] Other degrees of stress are subsumed under tone since every syllable bears a tone.' Full paper not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Uguru 2015/2014 treat Ika as a dialect of Igbo ('Ika Igbo', West Niger / Niger Igbo cluster) spoken in Ika South and Ika North East LGAs (Delta State) and Igbanke (Edo State); this is the same variety as Glottolog ikaa1238 / ISO ikk. Speaker in the JIPA Illustration is the author (one female speaker); the Wikipedia article names Akumuzi, Owa and Agbor dialects but the sources do not specify which was recorded.

tone_statements.citation: Manfredi, Victor. 1991. Ágbò̩ & É̩hu̩gbò: Ìgbo linguistic consciousness, its origins & limits. PhD dissertation (Committee on Linguistics and Social Anthropology), Harvard University, Cambridge MA, May 1991 [author's corrected 'compact edition', August 1991, 400 pp; PDF on the author's site].
tone_statements.quote: 1.3.3 Tone typology and innovations. Tone shift. In the dialects other than Ònìchà below, rightward tone shift has taken place at the word levels (cf. also 'navel' in 27c above); it is a common Igboid innovation. [table (36): 'bird', 'tortoise', 'man', 'cloth', 'tooth' in dialect columns headed Ágbò̩, Àbò̩, Ònìchà, É̩hu̩gbò, other] ... At the phrase level, (37) shows that downstepped high tone is affected by to tone shift, but the [dialect name lost in text layer] data show that the tone shift interacts with a process that relates downstep and low tone, as well as with a process that deletes a tone bearing unit. In order to clarify the complex correspondences in (37), both syntchronically and diachronically, it is necessary to view phrase-level downstep in a wider comparative context, in terms of an explanatory representation of tonal domains.

sources.note: Typology: H-spreading excludes total downstep, L-spreading excludes partial downstep but is prerequisite to total downstep; downstep as metrical constituency ('prosodic government'); Igbo(id) associative-construction downstep as a H-tone clitic; third verb tone class in Igboid. Same text as dissertation pp. 61-93.

sources.citation: Manfredi, Victor. 1992. The limits of downstep in Ágbò̩ sentence prosody. In Mark Liberman & Cynthia McLemore (eds.), Proceedings of the IRCS Workshop on Prosody in Natural Speech (IRCS Report 92-37), 103-115. Philadelphia: Institute for Research in Cognitive Science, University of Pennsylvania.
sources.note: First-hand instrumental/analytic study of downstep, downstep reset ('upstep'/antidownstep) and their syntactic conditioning in Ágbò̩ (Ika) sentences: per the author's summary on his page, 'so-called "upstep" is epiphenomenal.. no more than the phonetic realization of antidownstep (downstep reset), a phenomenon itself constrained by syntactic phrasing', with 81 transcribed and recorded Ágbò̩ examples. Presupposes the H/L + downstep system. The only dedicated tone/prosody paper on Ika besides Uguru's intonation work.

sources.citation: Manfredi, Victor. 1982. Centre and periphery in Ìká literacy. JOLAN: Journal of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria 1: 175-195.
sources.note: Literacy essay with incidental first-hand tonal remarks: underlying high and low tones, word-final falling tones, a low-tone subject concord marker surfacing as a low pronoun or as downstep before the verb stem (p. 182), 'four consecutive downsteps' (fn. 4); no tone count or TBU. No word stress.

tone.quote: Some phonological 'troughs' separating Ìka from its eastern neighbours and uniting it with Ẹ̀do (at least phon-aesthetically) include syllabic nasalization ...; deletion of a mora of vocalic length in word-boundary assimilations ...; a nine-vowel system; word-final falling tones. The mora deletion interacts with pitch adjustment rules to produce a greater degree of overlapping between underlying high and low tones, yielding a system more like the quasi-accentual downstep of Ẹ̀do. ... In this paper high toned syllables are unmarked
